name: Erik Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, independent of AI companies, employers, unions, parties and government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and have managed a six-person store-opening team for a large furniture retailer since last winter. Before that I spent years on the floor fitting displays and checking deliveries; now I have to sign off budgets and opening dates, and my deputy catches mistakes I still make in the cost sheets. I have a bachelor’s degree, but I am a junior at this kind of managing. I like walking into a new store and seeing the ramps and shelves in the places we promised.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and what other work could you reach?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Zara works at the public library, our children are adults and live elsewhere, and we still have a small mortgage. My pay is high for this manager job because long service and regional travel are in the contract; we have about fifteen months of expenses saved. Several retail chains operate nearby. I have never used AI myself and prefer the old opening checklist; I would need a trusted colleague to show me why a new tool was worth using.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my team to check the loading door before announcing delivery. A store does not open because a planning sheet says shelves have arrived. I still want a photograph and a person at the loading door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company will keep opening stores and my role should stay, though I am still the least seasoned manager in the region. Fifteen months saved and our small mortgage make a slow technology story manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next week I’d continue the Thursday walk-through with my deputy and tick each ramp and delivery bay against the signed opening list. In the first year I’d keep the reserve in cash and request my pension provider’s access date and net monthly estimate before discussing retirement with Zara.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about work and bills. I do not feel ready to stop working just because I am close to sixty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which opening nearly went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One ramp was on the drawing but the delivery crew had stored shelving across it. We moved the boxes before a wheelchair user had to discover the problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a new planning tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on my own. The existing list works when we walk the site, and I have not seen the new tool prove otherwise.

say: I’d require **loading-door proof** before calling shelves delivered.
I’d walk every **ramp and bay** before opening a store.
think: My **opening role** should continue in a plateau.
Fifteen months saved and a **small mortgage** make ordinary setbacks manageable.
do: Keep the **Thursday walk-through** and check ramps against the signed list.
Hold the **cash reserve** and request actual pension access and net income before retirement talk.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and household bills.
S0.quote: A store does not open because a planning sheet says shelves have arrived.
fieldNote: He has **high contract pay** despite being a new, error-prone manager.
A **fifteen-month reserve** gives him room to wait for verified figures.
He has **never used AI** and relies on site checks and his deputy.

steps.text: Keep Thursday site walk-through with deputy and check ramps and delivery bays
Request pension provider’s access date and net monthly estimate before discussing retirement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the retailer that software can plan openings and order stock, but it cannot know a ramp is blocked unless someone checks. I would not send a completion notice before the store lead signs the site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Schedules, orders and budgets fill my new job, so the company could put one manager over several openings. My deputy is better with the numbers; if they cut a post, mine is hardly untouchable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d ask the property lead to test one AI opening plan against a store we just finished, with the deputy checking every listed fixture. I’d keep our manual signoff in the first year and consider the tool only if it correctly flags the blocked-ramp case and the property lead explains who can halt a wrong opening; I’d ask for written staffing dates if regions are merged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about my own post, though the savings keep us from making a rushed move. I would rather look slow than open a store with an unusable ramp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the tool if it passes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch my deputy run one live opening with the property lead first. I would not learn it on a customer’s first morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your deputy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say their eye for the numbers is why I want them on the check. I will not pretend I know more than the person who catches my errors.

say: I’d keep **site signoff** before any store completion notice.
An AI opening plan must catch the **blocked ramp** before I trust it.
think: One manager could cover **several openings** if planning is automated.
My deputy’s stronger budget work makes **my junior post** vulnerable.
do: Ask for a **one-store comparison** with deputy fixture checks.
Keep **manual signoff** in the first year; consider AI only after ramp proof and a named halt authority.
Watch a **deputy-led live opening** before using the tool myself.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my own role.
S1.quote: I would rather look slow than open a store with an unusable ramp.
fieldNote: He acknowledges the deputy’s **stronger budget skill**.
He would watch a **trusted colleague** before personally using AI.
His own manager role contains **exposed planning work**.

steps.text: Ask property lead and deputy to compare AI plan with one finished store
Keep manual site signoff; consider AI only after blocked-ramp proof and named halt authority
Watch deputy run a live opening with property lead before personally using AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the retailer for a written date and terms if opening teams shrink. Store staff should know whom to call when an automated plan says the delivery is complete but the bay is empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could plan openings, buy fixtures and settle budgets better than I can, so I expect this junior post to end around sixty. Zara’s library queries and cataloguing face the same thinking AI then; shelving is physical until robots around 2031, but her pay alone would not cover our mortgage and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask the pension provider for written age-sixty access and net-income figures and ask HR for notice terms without treating severance as cash. Before 2028 I’d ask local retailers which paid store-floor supervisor vacancies are posted; in the first year after AGI I’d accept one only if its written wage plus Zara’s actual pay covers our mortgage and bills, the work includes paid on-site checks, and I can manage the standing hours. If no wage or verified pension covers the gap, I’d keep looking rather than call sixty retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed by the prospect of both salaries changing, even with fifteen months saved. The reserve gives us search time, not a wage for the next decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the floor supervisor job be safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Its orders and rotas face 2028 AGI too. The shelf and ramp checks may need a person until robots arrive around 2031, so it is a paid bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop the extra weekend trips to our daughter’s city if both wages fell. I would call her, not make her pay for the trip.

say: I’d demand **written team-closure terms** and a contact for empty bays.
Store staff need a **human delivery answer** when a plan says stock arrived.
think: I expect **my junior post** to end around sixty.
Zara’s library thinking work faces **2028 AGI**, and her pay alone cannot cover our bills.
do: Request **written pension figures** and notice terms without assuming severance.
Seek **posted floor work**; accept only with written pay plus Zara’s earnings covering mortgage and bills, paid checks and tolerable standing.
Cut **extra weekend travel** if both salaries fall.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about both incomes despite cash.
S2.quote: The reserve gives us search time, not a wage for the next decade.
fieldNote: His own planning job faces **2028 AGI** directly.
Library cataloguing also faces AGI before **2031 shelving robots**.
A floor role needs **written pay**, actual partner income, paid site checks and tolerable hours.

steps.text: Ask provider and HR for written age-sixty pension access and job notice terms
Ask nearby retailers about posted paid store-floor supervisor vacancies before 2028
Accept floor role with written pay plus Zara’s earnings covering mortgage, paid checks and workable hours
Stop extra weekend trips if both salaries fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years lets the retailer post real floor jobs and pay people to learn a safe opening check. I would not promise the store-floor route lasts forever when robots come later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At about 63, a pension may be accessible, but I need the provider’s net figure before deciding whether I can stop earning. Opening plans and even a floor supervisor’s orders face 2031 AGI; physical fixture checks face robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In January 2027 Zara and I would set aside 180 monthly for an income gap only while both wages arrive and the fifteen-month reserve remains intact. I’d ask a local chain for a paid supervised opening-check shift before 2031 and apply for a posted floor role only if written pay and shifts with Zara’s actual earnings cover our mortgage and bills; after AGI I’d stay only while human site checks remain paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious but not cornered. Five years lets me see a real roster before leaving this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the trial shift teach you a new trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would show whether I can stand through an opening and use that chain’s checklist. I would ask for paid hours and a supervisor, not a certificate in a folder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Zara’s library hours change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the 180 transfer stops. My partner Zara’s actual library wages count, not the job title printed on a card.

say: I’d ask for **posted floor wages** and paid supervised opening checks.
A floor role is no **permanent shelter** from later robots.
think: My **pension at 63** needs a net figure before I can stop earning.
Floor orders face **2031 AGI** before 2034 fixture robots.
do: Save **180 monthly** only while both wages and the reserve hold.
Ask for a **paid supervised shift**; apply only for posted floor wages and shifts plus Zara’s earnings covering mortgage and bills.
Stay after AGI only while **human fixture checks** are paid.
feel: I feel **anxious** but can inspect real rosters.
S3.quote: My partner Zara’s actual library wages count, not the job title printed on a card.
fieldNote: A paid supervised shift tests **standing and checklist fit**, not a promised transfer.
His pension is **unverified at 63** despite strong savings.
He accepts that floor planning remains **thinking work** exposed to AGI.

steps.text: Save 180 monthly only while both wages arrive and fifteen-month reserve stays intact
Ask local chain for paid supervised opening-check shift before 2031
Apply only for posted floor role with written wages and shifts plus Zara’s earnings covering bills
Stay in paid human site checks after 2031 only while offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the retailer that a decade is enough to give people a real staffing calendar and a pension contact, not a goodbye speech. I would keep the site checklist available to anyone who must sign an opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 in 2036. If my pension and Zara’s then-current income are accessible and sufficient, I might leave paid work, but a birthday by itself buys nothing; opening budgets face 2036 AGI, and physical store checks face robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Each January starting in 2027 I’d request an updated pension access and net-income estimate and compare it with our remaining mortgage and bills. I’d keep a paid retail role while it exists and consider stopping only if the provider confirms spendable income plus Zara’s actual income then covers housing, health and daily costs; in the first year after AGI I’d take posted paid floor work if that income falls short and the chain still pays for human fixture checks, otherwise keep seeking paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m uneasy about the title disappearing, but the longer runway lets us see actual numbers. I will not turn fifteen months of cash into an imaginary lifetime salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pension estimate falls short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I keep looking for paid work at local chains. We can use some reserve between jobs, but I will not promise Zara that it can carry us for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your children to support you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. They have their own lives, and the provider’s numbers must work without their wages.

Store signers need the **site checklist** after any staffing change.
think: At **68 in 2036**, retirement needs spendable pension and Zara’s actual income.
Opening budgets face **2036 AGI** before 2039 robots reach fixture checks.
do: Request **updated pension figures** and compare them with mortgage and bills each January.
Keep **paid retail work** until verified pension and Zara’s income cover housing, health and daily costs.
After AGI, take **posted paid floor work** if income falls short and checks are funded; seek other pay if no post exists.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about title loss despite planning time.
S4.quote: I will not turn fifteen months of cash into an imaginary lifetime salary.
fieldNote: His strong reserve is a **job-search bridge**, not permanent retirement income.
A floor job requires **paid human checks** even after 2036.
Adult children’s wages stay **outside retirement calculations**.

steps.text: Request annual written pension access and net-income figures against mortgage and bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because both opening plans and Zara’s library work could shrink at once. Written pension and job terms, and an actual paid floor vacancy with sensible hours, would let us decide without panic. I have fifteen months saved, not fifteen years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether I am embarrassed when my deputy corrects a budget. Sometimes I am. I can live with my deputy correcting a budget; I cannot live with signing a store open while its ramp is blocked.

headlineQuote: I can live with my deputy correcting a budget; I cannot live with signing a store open while its ramp is blocked.
portrait: **Erik**, 58, is a new junior store-opening manager after years fitting displays.
His bachelor’s degree and long service bring **high pay**, but the deputy still catches budget errors.
He has **fifteen months saved**, a small mortgage and several local retail employers.
He has **never used AI** and needs a trusted colleague’s demonstration before considering it.
He treats a floor role as **paid temporary work** and pension access as unverified.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could shrink both his opening job and Zara’s library work before pension income is confirmed.
whatWouldHelp: **Written terms** for pension and jobs, plus a paid floor vacancy with workable hours, would help.
